"Devoid" means completely without something — not just low on it, or barely having it, but having absolutely none of it. It describes a total, complete absence.

Think of an empty bottle. If a bottle is devoid of water, it doesn't mean there's a little water left at the bottom. It means there is none at all. That's the key: devoid describes zero, not near-zero.

"Devoid" never stands alone. It always pairs with the word "of," and the structure is always:

[something] is devoid of [something else]

That "of" introduces what is missing. So:

  • "The speech was devoid of humor" — the speech had no humor whatsoever.
  • "His eyes were devoid of emotion" — his eyes showed absolutely no emotion.
  • "The painting was devoid of color" — the painting was entirely colorless.

Without "of," the word is incomplete. You can never call something simply "devoid" and stop there — you always have to say devoid of what.
Where it sits in a sentence

"Devoid" is placed after the noun it describes, not before it. You say "a life devoid of meaning" or "her voice was devoid of warmth" — never "a devoid life" or "her devoid voice." The phrase "devoid of [something]" must always follow the noun, either directly or through a linking verb like is, was, or seemed.
The most important nuance: total absence

This is what separates "devoid" from weaker words like "lacking." When you say something is devoid of something, you are making an absolute claim — that the thing is entirely gone, not just in short supply.

Compare these two sentences: "The film lacked excitement" suggests it could have been more thrilling — it had some excitement, but not enough. "The film was devoid of excitement" means there was no excitement from the first scene to the last. Not a drop. The difference matters, and choosing "devoid" is a deliberate, strong choice.
What kinds of things can be "devoid of"?

Devoid is most naturally used when the missing thing is a quality, feeling, or characteristic — something abstract rather than a physical object. It fits perfectly with emotions and feelings (empathy, warmth, compassion, joy), with intellectual or moral qualities (logic, purpose, originality, substance, integrity), and with atmospheric or aesthetic qualities (color, life, hope, meaning, imagination).

Saying "the office was devoid of chairs" is grammatically possible but sounds stiff and unusual. Saying "the office was devoid of humanity" feels completely natural. The word belongs to the world of the abstract and the intangible — the things you can feel or sense but not pick up and hold.

"Devoid" has a formal, serious, and often cold or critical tone. When someone calls something "devoid of" a quality, they are usually pointing out that something is missing which should be there — implying a deficiency, a flaw, or a troubling emptiness.

"Her apology was devoid of sincerity" doesn't just describe the apology as insincere — it makes that insincerity feel stark and complete, like there wasn't even a trace of genuineness in it.

"The city streets were devoid of life" doesn't just say the streets were quiet — it conjures something eerie, abandoned, and hollow.

Because of this weight and formality, "devoid" appears most often in written English — in essays, journalism, literary fiction, and criticism — rather than in everyday conversation. In casual speech, someone would say "this soup has no flavor" rather than "this soup is devoid of flavor." But in writing, "devoid" is precise and carries real punch.
How it compares to similar words

Without is the neutral, everyday equivalent. "Without hope" is simply factual and flat. "Devoid of hope" is stronger — it stresses the completeness of the absence and adds weight.

Lacking can describe a partial deficiency. "Lacking confidence" might mean someone has some confidence, just not enough. "Devoid of confidence" means they have none at all.

Empty usually describes physical space — an empty room, an empty stomach. "Devoid" reaches into the abstract and describes emptiness of character, feeling, or quality, which is why it sounds more literary and precise.

Void of is an older, rarer phrasing that means exactly the same thing. You'll encounter it in older texts, but "devoid of" is the standard form today.

"Devoid of" means completely without — with absolutely none of the named quality present. It is formal, emphatic, and almost always signals that something is not just low on a quality, but has none of it whatsoever. It always needs "of" after it, it always signals a total absence (never a partial one), and it almost always carries a serious, often critical tone. Use it when you want to make it unmistakably clear that something is entirely, completely, thoroughly without a thing.
